title: How to test language and accent realism in training simulations
summary: Evaluate training simulations across languages and accents by checking speech, recognition and feedback separately with relevant local reviewers.
body_markdown:
A convincing demonstration in one language does not establish that a simulation will work for every team. Test the customer voice, the learner's speech and the resulting feedback separately, using the language and regional context of the work you intend to train.


## Define the language requirement precisely


List the language of the customer conversation, the regional vocabulary customers use, the language learners prefer for feedback and any written material they must read. Treat these as separate requirements. A familiar voice can still use the wrong terminology, and accurate speech recognition does not by itself establish useful coaching.


Recruit reviewers who know the language and the job. Ask them to assess intelligibility and meaning without treating one accent as the standard of competence. If understanding unfamiliar customer accents is a learning objective, describe the actual customer situations involved rather than making an accent a shorthand for difficulty.


## Run a small set of controlled comparisons


Start with the same task and expected outcome across language variants. Include ordinary phrasing, relevant regional terms, names, dates, amounts and a natural correction during the conversation. Add code-switching only if it is part of the real work. Ask whether each requirement is supported before spending time building the test.


Have representative learners complete the exercise using their normal equipment. Check the recording against any available transcript and feedback. Record whether an error began with speech recognition, the simulated customer's response or the assessment. If you cannot inspect enough evidence to locate the problem, record that limitation instead of attributing it to the learner.


## Use a language acceptance matrix


Use this checklist for each language and regional variant you plan to use. Keep unresolved questions visible; a result from an English demonstration should not fill a blank in another language.


Requirement Test Record


Customer speech Have local reviewers hear the scenario and its follow-up responses. Natural wording, comprehensibility and any misleading pronunciation.


Learner recognition Complete the same task with representative speakers. Meaning preserved or lost, with the affected words and recording reference.


Conversation behavior Correct a detail, ask for clarification and use relevant terminology. Whether the response follows the intended meaning.


Assessment and coaching Compare feedback with a qualified review of the recording. Unsupported deductions, missing evidence and language of feedback.


Decision Review findings with the training owner. Accepted, needs retesting or unsuitable for this workflow, plus owner and date.


## A fictional example: an address correction


A delivery support team evaluates a Spanish-language exercise in which a customer corrects an apartment number. The learner repeats the corrected number and updates the fictional record. A local reviewer hears the correct response, but the transcript retains the first number and the feedback marks the learner down.


The team records a recognition problem rather than a failure to follow the process. It tests a different address and another speaker, then asks the provider how the discrepancy can be reviewed. This keeps the evaluation focused on whether the exercise can assess the intended skill reliably.


## Keep approval specific to what you tested


Approve the tested language, workflow and conditions together. Document any manual review needed and the remaining gaps before expanding the rollout. Ask the provider to demonstrate requested regional voices, recognition and feedback capabilities; do not infer their availability from a broad language list. Retest meaningful changes with local reviewers and keep their observations alongside the acceptance decision.
